title: Why You Must Never Limit Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case against a common instinct: restricting the freedoms of difficult students, such as permanently isolating their desks or barring them from working with certain classmates. He distinguishes these open-ended limits from legitimate, time-bound consequences, arguing that limits are punitive in a way that never ends and never teaches. The article lists three specific harms of limiting difficult students: it labels them permanently, it instills a fixed rather than growth mindset, and it denies them the chance to ever improve because avoidance replaces real teaching. Instead, he calls for clear boundaries, close supervision, and consistent accountability paired with a visible willingness to trust students again after they've served a consequence. The piece frames this trust-building as a slow, daily process of showing belief in students' capacity to change.
points: Permanently restricting a difficult student's freedoms (seating, groupings, activities) differs from and is worse than enforcing a predetermined, time-bound consequence.
Limiting a student's opportunities sends the message that they are permanently defective, which reinforces misbehavior rather than reducing it.
Static limits instill a fixed mindset in students by communicating they cannot change or improve.
Avoidance strategies, like banning a student from group work permanently, prevent students from ever getting the practice needed to improve.
Real change comes from a steady, daily accumulation of trust, accountability, and second chances rather than one dramatic intervention.
quotes: Now, it’s important to point out that this isn’t the same as enforcing consequences , which are predetermined, sharply defined, and time constrained.
You’re saying to them that they don’t measure up and that ‘behavior problem’ is who they are. They’re unbridled, even inhuman, and unable to control their emotions.
A growth mindset is the belief you can improve. You’re not stuck in your current station but instead through hard work and determination can change and better yourself and your circumstances.
When you tell students that they can no longer play soccer on the playground because they’re too aggressive and can’t control their anger, then they never get better.
Avoidance isn’t a classroom management strategy. What they need are clear boundaries, accountability, and the opportunity to try again—and again and again.
The lessons learned from knowing exactly what is expected, and being held strictly accountable to those expectations, over time, if given the opportunity to learn from mistakes, changes behavior.
